rv.q: Still, this is a first-hand, on-the-ground, observational theatre done with great wit.

It never preaches, but hits hard at the pomposity and thoughtless actions of the past: a cleverly sobering device for a predominantly British audience to absorb. Shehada is an amiable and energetic performer who wants to entertain as well as inform.

Its attention to Britain's own historical responsibility is particularly interesting. Between scenes, recordings of British political statements from 1917 to 1919 interrupt the storytelling. It is a clever directorial decision: just as we settle into Shehada's characters, we are confronted with the language of historical wrongdoing.
Shehada and Beale pull it off flawlessly, offering a show as gag-packed as any top-shelf comedy.
Shehada has a natural instinct for crowd-work that is a joy to watch and participate in, and his physical comedy is charming.
